items.content:
Despite US-Israeli airstrikes and Tehran’s attacks on shipping, the waterway still has to provide a lifeline for those that live and work there
By Stefanie Glinski ; photographs by Mohammad Mohsenifar in Bandar Abbas/on Hormuz Island
Capt Farouq turns the wheel as he watches the ferry terminal of Bandar Abbas grow smaller, its bright lights flickering in the distance.
In front of him, the navigation radar beeps periodically, its green and pink lights glowing in the darkness. The ferry, today at about half capacity with roughly 100 passengers, turns and heads into the darkness of the strait of Hormuz.
He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home
Farouq, 39, sits comfortably in his cabin, overlooking the pitch black horizon as he sails towards Hormuz Island, a short commute of about half an hour from the Iranian mainland’s Haqqani Port, for 340,000 toman, about £1. He is relaxed and smiles as he pulls into the deeper waters. He’s been a captain for the past 18 years, and the strait of Hormuz is his second home.
Farouq says the crossings have not stopped since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on 28 February, although passenger numbers are down and the journey has become more dangerous. For months, Farouq has heard explosions coming from the strait, unclear as to whether that is air defence or attacks, or both. Tonight is no different.
Inside the ferry, passengers say they have gotten used to the sounds too, and, to an extent, the war itself. They drink tea and smoke cigarettes. Some nap, while others entertain their children. It’s hot and humid, the air thick, the windows fogged with condensation.
Even with a fragile ceasefire in place, here on the coast, it has barely felt as though the war has stopped.
According to Iranian government sources, attacks on the southern port of Bandar Abbas have damaged 760 fishing and commercial vessels. Farouq says his own ferry was also damaged by shrapnel while docked at the port, though it was quickly repaired.
Since the start of the war, Iranian forces have repeatedly attacked vessels attempting to cross the strait. In the first week of October alone, at least 12 attacks were reported against oil, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, sending oil prices back above $100 a barrel .
With pressure mounting on the US president, Donald Trump, before the midterm elections, he is rumoured to be once again considering strikes.
But beyond the headlines and global markets, the strait is first and foremost a lifeline for many Iranians living in the southern province of Hormozgan.
Fishers in Bandar Abbas selling their catch on the street
Fishers, captains and harbour workers all depend on the strait for their livelihoods and the war has made their work increasingly difficult. Fishers can no longer venture as far out, ports have come under attack, and many people fled Bandar Abbas in the early months of the war for smaller, more remote villages in search of safety.
Local residents fishing for their own daily consumption
Anvar Sadat, a 38-year-old fisher who works at Bandar Abbas’s fish market, says business has slowed and that making ends meet has become increasingly difficult.
“Fishing boats can’t go out as freely as before the war, and our movement is restricted,” he says, adding that several of his colleagues in the city have been killed in attacks.
Anvar Sadat, who works at the fish market in Bandar Abbas
“This place was hell,” says Abdul Salam, a 45-year-old garbage collector. The beaches, particularly those near the port, were among the most dangerous places during the height of the war, he says, describing heavy attacks that forced him to stop working almost entirely to avoid the risk.
Life on the island, however, has been different, Farouq explains as he steers into the small, dimly lit port of Hormuz Island, his last crossing of the day before heading back to his family for the night.
Hassan, 28, cafe owner – has run a cafe on the island for eight years
Hormuz Island has long been known as a kind of “hippy paradise”, a place Iranians have come to regard as “free”. Artists and creatives moved here from bigger cities in search of peace; women swim in bathing suits, writers and painters find space to work, and life moves slower. There is “love and magic” here, as Yashar, a 35-year-old surfer, puts it, “a different rhythm”.
A group of local women swimming off the coast of Hormuz Island
Life here has changed little, Yashar says, although the war has brought some new restrictions, and a handful of attacks, mostly on infrastructure. The roughly 8,000 residents are trying to support each other, and to preserve the sense of freedom that has set the island apart, he adds.
The government has closed off parts of Hormuz Island’s north, but beyond the now restricted areas, life has continued, he explains. “As long as you don’t go north, they leave you alone,” he says of the army.
Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide – the tourism sector has been hit by the conflict
The Majara hotel, also known as Rainbow accommodation, is one of Hormuz’s attractions. It has been closed since the beginning of the war
“The tourism sector has taken the biggest hit,” says Omran, a 45-year-old tour guide, adding that he prefers to go by his first name only. “Guesthouses and homestays remain closed, as do restaurants and many cafes.” Visitors have largely stopped coming since the war, dealing a heavy blow to an island whose economy depends on tourism and fishing, both of which have been disrupted.
The Salt valley on Hormuz Island, one of the island’s tourist attractions
From the higher parts of the island, Omran says, it is possible to see deep into the strait on clear days, when the haze lifts and the humid air clears, all the way to the mountains of Khasab in Oman.
Residents have climbed up these barren mountains of red and white stone, at times watching the war unfold in the distance. Tankers remain stranded in the strait, explosions can be heard regularly. Yet residents also say the war has not driven them from the island.
Khaleh Kaniz, a 67-year-old painter who was born and raised on Hormuz, laughs when asked whether she had considered leaving in February, at the start of the war.
“Why should we leave? Where would we go? Our homes and our lives are here.”

(Kitco NewsWire) – Spot  gold prices were slightly higher and spot  silver prices were lower in early U.S. trading Wednesday, as renewed concerns about energy supplies through the Strait of Hormuz and persistent expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening weighed on precious metals. Gold found some support from lower Treasury yields and defensive demand, while silver struggled to sustain Tuesday's recovery amid uncertainty surrounding industrial activity and the interest rate outlook. At the time of the latest verified morning price reading, spot gold was trading near $4,136.70 an ounce, up $12.60, or 0.31%, while spot silver was trading near $57.510, down $0.370, or 0.64%.
Market positioning remains divided between signs of weakening economic activity and stubborn inflation pressure. September consumer prices increased 0.6% on the month and 3.7% annually, while producer prices surged 1.3% and 6.3%, respectively. Despite those inflation surprises, traders continue to assign approximately an 83% probability that the Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its Oct. 27-28 meeting. Expectations for another rate increase remain concentrated in December, with futures indicating roughly a 94% probability that rates will be higher by the Dec. 9 meeting. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield was trading near the 5.1% area Wednesday morning, down from recent highs above 5.3%, as weaker housing activity and concerns about financial-market stability supported government bonds. The dollar's broader resilience and the prospect of additional Fed tightening continue to limit gold's upside potential despite some relief from lower yields.
The Federal Reserve remains in its premeeting communications blackout, leaving incoming economic releases and energy-market developments as the principal drivers of interest rate expectations. Wednesday's calendar includes the weekly U.S. petroleum inventory report at 10:30 a.m. EDT and a 20-year Treasury bond auction at 1 p.m. EDT. Thursday brings weekly initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. EDT, followed Friday by preliminary October manufacturing and services purchasing managers' indexes at 9:45 a.m. EDT and the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment reading at 10 a.m. EDT. Softer employment and business activity figures could reinforce concerns about slowing growth and reduce December tightening expectations, supporting gold through lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar. However, persistently elevated inflation expectations or renewed energy-price increases would strengthen the case for additional Fed tightening and maintain pressure on non-yielding bullion.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remains a significant source of volatility in global energy and precious metals markets. Oil prices rebounded Wednesday following reports of additional attacks on commercial shipping in the strategic waterway, while Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi signaled that prospects for a near-term peace agreement with Washington remain limited. The latest escalation followed Tuesday's sharp intraday reversal in crude prices amid conflicting reports about potential diplomatic negotiations. The underlying supply situation remains fragile despite a recovery in overall Middle Eastern crude exports. Regional oil shipments averaged approximately 24.6 million barrels per day in the week ending Oct. 18, exceeding the prewar average of 23.3 million barrels per day as producers expanded alternative export routes. However, shipments directly through Hormuz remained approximately 33% below prewar levels, while attacks on vessels and infrastructure continued to threaten the reliability of regional energy supplies. Brent crude climbed back above $110.00 a barrel Wednesday, reinforcing concerns about the inflationary consequences of a prolonged regional conflict.
For gold, continued uncertainty surrounding Gulf security supports defensive demand, but higher crude prices also reinforce inflation expectations and the prospect of restrictive U.S. monetary policy. This competing influence helps explain why bullion has struggled to sustain rallies despite the continuing geopolitical conflict. Silver faces similar interest rate headwinds, with its industrial exposure adding sensitivity to signs of weaker economic activity. The prospect of further Fed tightening, alongside uncertainty about the direction of oil prices, continues to complicate the near-term outlook for both metals.
Global equity markets were mixed to firmer before the U.S. open, with technology shares recovering amid a fresh round of corporate earnings. Nasdaq futures advanced approximately 0.4% and S&P 500 futures gained 0.2%, while Dow futures were little changed. Asian markets were generally firmer, with South Korea's Kospi gaining approximately 3.3% and Japan's Nikkei 225 advancing as investors returned to semiconductor and artificial intelligence-related shares. European markets were mixed, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 near unchanged, Germany's DAX slightly lower and France's CAC 40 posting modest gains. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 weakened amid pressure on mining shares. Investors are also assessing quarterly corporate results and the implications of elevated financing costs for technology-sector investment, while continuing fiscal uncertainty in France has kept European government bond markets under pressure.

items.title: Rosenberg: US diplomatic push offers little hope for imminent Ukraine peace
items.summary: President Vladimir Putin does not feel under pressure right now to end the war, the BBC's Russia Editor writes.
items.content:
Image caption, Witkoff (R) said there was still important work to do after the meeting with Putin (L)
By Steve Rosenberg Russia Editor ,Â  Reporting from Moscow
After two days of diplomacy â in Norway's capital and Russia's St Petersburg â is the war in Ukraine any closer to ending?
"Good and constructive" is how Norway's prime minister described Tuesday's talks between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and European representatives.
In Oslo, the idea of a trilateral meeting at leaders' level was floated. The hope was that Steve Witkoff's trip to Russia would pave the way for President Vladimir Putin, Zelensky and Trump to meet and agree an end to the fighting.
But Putin has shown little desire to share a table with Zelensky - unless that table is in Moscow.
The Kremlin says it may be willing to resume trilateral talks next month in Abu Dhabi, but only at the technical level.
In a post on X, Steve Witkoff himself conceded that "there is still important work to do", though he claimed "President Trump remains committed to seeing this war end..."
Russia says it is ready to resume talks with Ukraine and US to end war
Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
US citizen Stephen Hubbard freed by Russia as Trump envoy meets Putin
For me, the most telling statement of the day was from Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov. He took part in the St Petersburg talks.
Ushakov said that Steve Witkoff had told President Putin about the discussions in Oslo and (as Witkoff viewed them) "new approaches from the Europeans and Kyiv".
The Kremlin adviser was clearly unimpressed by what he heard.
"In terms of resolving the Ukraine crisis, there wasn't much there that was useful," commented Ushakov.
Later Russian state TV asked him about the prospects for peace.
"I don't know how close we are getting," Yuri Ushakov said, "but things are moving in that direction."
It seems that President Putin doesn't feel under pressure right now to end the war.
He knows that Ukraine's air defences are under severe strain.
He knows that winter is coming and may well view the cold weather as an opportunity to pound Ukraine into submission.
He knows, too, that there is a US president in the White House who clearly wants a bigger, better, more profitable relationship with Moscow.
Image caption, Despite a "constructive" meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky in Oslo, Norway, the idea of a US-Russia-Ukraine trilateral summit does not seem to have taken hold
In recent days Donald Trump has paused some sanctions on Moscow, has agreed to buy Russian diesel and expressed biting criticism of President Zelensky.
That suits Russia just fine. It eases the pressure on the Kremlin leader.
"Right now Trump is the only leader in the Western world who is doing something for peace," Russian MP and TV anchor Evgeny Popov says.
"Doing something for peace, but a peace on your terms?" I respond. "Is that what you want?"
A Putin-Zelensky-Trump trilateral may not be imminent.
But in China next month a meeting between Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping may well take place on the fringes of the Apec summit.
Some commentators here are already dubbing it "The New Yalta" - a reference to the Yalta Conference of 1945, where Stalin, Churchill and Roosevelt met to plan the political and territorial reorganisation of post-war Europe.
"Russia, China and the United States are the only superpowers right now in the world," Evgeny Popov says. "Of course, it will be good for the entire world if our leaders meet in China."
After nearly five years of war, that would put Vladimir Putin exactly where he wants to be - at the top table of global politics.

Gold Declines Towards $4,120 as Iran Conflict and Federal Reserve Outlook Remain in Focus
Gold coin ©PIX1861 Gold prices declined on Wednesday as investors assessed uncertainty surrounding efforts to end the conflict between the United States and Iran, alongside expectations for US interest rates and the potential inflationary effects of higher energy costs.
At 02:36 ET (06:36 GMT), spot gold was down 0.2% at $4,117.31 per ounce, while US gold futures fell 0.2% to $4,134.92 per ounce.
Other precious metals also traded lower. Silver declined 1.2% to $57.2955 per ounce, platinum lost 1.8% to $1,627.45, and spot palladium decreased 1.6% to $1,088.40.
The US Dollar Index edged up 0.1% to 101.80, adding to the market conditions affecting dollar-denominated commodities.
Gold has fallen more than 1% since the beginning of the week and remains approximately 20% below its level when the US-Iran conflict began in late February.
The conflict has disrupted energy supplies and contributed to higher oil prices, complicating the inflation outlook and expectations for monetary policy.
Higher interest rates can affect demand for gold because the metal does not generate interest income, making interest-bearing assets comparatively more attractive.
Oil Price Movements Reflect Uncertainty Over Iran Negotiations
Oil prices stabilised on Wednesday after retreating from a five-month high during the previous session.
The decline followed reports suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to an agreement to end the conflict. However, a diplomat subsequently dismissed suggestions that a settlement was imminent.
Gold prices initially increased as oil declined following the reports of possible negotiations, before reversing those gains when energy prices recovered.
The US dollar and government bond yields also moved lower during the period of fluctuating oil prices.
Market participants continued to assess the potential implications of the conflict for global energy supplies, inflation and economic activity.
The relationship between energy prices and inflation expectations remains particularly relevant to gold, given the influence of monetary policy expectations on demand for non-interest-bearing assets.
US Treasury securities with longer maturities gained as oil prices retreated and economic data indicated softer conditions in parts of the US economy.
September housing starts declined, while pending home sales fell to a record low, providing further evidence of reduced activity in the housing market.
The figures added to the economic information being considered ahead of the Federal Reserve's next monetary policy meeting, scheduled for 27–28 October.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh's comments on Friday did not materially change market expectations for the upcoming decision.
Investors continued to anticipate that the central bank would leave its benchmark interest rate unchanged at the October meeting.
Market pricing indicated a probability of less than 17% that the Fed would increase rates by 25 basis points at that meeting.
However, inflation remains above the central bank's 2% target, and traders were assigning approximately an 85% probability to another interest rate increase before the end of the year.
Warsh's remarks came ahead of the Federal Reserve's communications blackout period, which begins on Saturday and restricts public commentary from policymakers before the meeting.
With limited additional guidance expected from central bank officials, investors are monitoring economic indicators, Treasury yields and developments in the Middle East for information that could influence interest rate expectations.
Gold and other precious metals remained under pressure during Wednesday's trading as markets continued to evaluate the interaction between energy prices, inflation and the Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook.

items.title: CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike and stock sinks
items.summary: CoreWeave shares are down 29% in October, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
items.content:
CoreWeave’s market confidence erodes as bond yields spike, stock sinks
CoreWeave's stock is down 29% this month, and the spreads in its credit default swaps are widening.
The company's elevated bond yield is prompting investors to question what additional financing options are available.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients this week, referring to AI bonds.
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator appears after the company's initial public offering at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on March 28, 2025.
CoreWeave is facing a crisis of confidence on Wall Street that's playing out in real time among equity and bond investors.
With interest rates spiking and AI build-out concerns mounting, debt-heavy neoclouds like CoreWeave are being viewed by many market participants as the most vulnerable trade in the artificial intelligence space.
"Sentiment is decidedly negative," Andrew Keches, a credit analyst at Barclays, wrote in a note to clients on Tuesday, referring broadly to corporate debt in tech. Keches highlighted the "speed at which AI vibes are shifting on a day-to-day basis."
CoreWeave, which went public in March of last year and reached a peak market cap of about $90 billion three months later, is now valued at roughly $34 billion, with its stock down 29% this month. Its unsecured debt, meanwhile, is sporting a yield of about 15%.
The spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps, which are insurance against default, is up 164% in the past year and 30% in October. It last stood at nearly 1,067 basis points, or 10.67%.
The story is playing out across the neocloud sector. Shares of Nebius are down 27% this month, while IREN's stock is down 32%. In Australia, shares of data center operator NextDC plunged 40% on Wednesday after the company slashed its annual earnings forecast. Earlier this month, Australian data center company Firmus scrapped its planned initial public offering, citing market volatility and conditions.
U.K. neocloud Nscale is now under the microscope as investors wait to see whether the Nvidia-backed company will go through with its IPO. The company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange last month.
CoreWeave is the biggest of the pack, and is intimately tied to the U.S. AI market. Nvidia is its top institutional investor, with a stake of about 9%, according to FactSet. And more than two-thirds of CoreWeave's revenue last year came from Microsoft .
That's put a spotlight on CoreWeave's financials and its ability to remain viable. The company has about $20.7 billion in debt coming due through 2030 and another $14.9 billion thereafter, with the prospects of higher interest rates on future financing.
Sources on credit desks told CNBC that the high-yield debt market is effectively on hold until after the midterm elections in two weeks given ongoing concerns about the political pushback that data centers are facing. One source, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the matter, said fixed income investors "want permitting and regulatory requirements to be substantially resolved" before they commit financing.
"Given recent turbulence, pausing makes sense," Seth Meyer, global head of client portfolio management at Janus Henderson, said in an interview.
CoreWeave CEO Mike Intrator, who co-founded the company in 2017 initially as a crypto-mining venture, sent a memo to employees on Thursday, which CNBC obtained, to try and tamp down concern. Intrator stressed that the company maintains a range of funding options.
"Our financing model combines infrastructure-backed borrowing, corporate debt, equity, and customer prepayments," Intrator wrote. He added that the company has "additional flexibility to raise equity over time as market conditions and our capital needs warrant."
CoreWeave had $5.5 billion of cash and equivalents at the end of the second quarter. The company is expected to report third-quarter results next month. Analysts expect negative free cash flow in the period to swell to $10.1 billion, the highest since the company started reporting quarterly financials, according to FactSet.
One issue being debated heading into the report is how much more capital CoreWeave needs to raise. Rob Oliver, a software analyst at Baird, is estimating roughly $30 billion in 2027.
"Earnings may address financing measures to shore up confidence," Oliver said in an interview. "But they wouldn't need that capital until the first quarter."
Another question is whether Nvidia will step in if necessary?
Nvidia, which supplies the graphics processing units that CoreWeave rents out, invested $2 billion in January for a 10% stake. The purchase price was $87.20 a share. The stock is now trading at $61.82 even after jumping 6% the day of the announcement.
While Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said last week that CoreWeave doesn't need a backstop, some investors say the chip giant's further participation may be necessary if credit conditions continue to worsen.
Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs , JPMorgan Chase and Barclays have put out bullish notes on the company this week, highlighting the company's GPU-backed loans and its solid list of investment-grade customers like Microsoft and Meta . Goldman analysts emphasized the company's strength in the market relative to many of its neocloud competitors.
"Not all neoclouds are created equal," they wrote, in upgrading their rating to buy from hold. "CoreWeave is likely in the top quartile of neoclouds, if not the top decile, when measured on performance and ability to execute."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox and Jordan Novet contributed to this report.

If a Stock Market Crash Is Coming, Warren Buffett Says This Is the Smartest Move Investors Can Make
After a year of record-breaking gains, major market indexes are wobbling. The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has fallen by nearly 2% over the last week, as of this writing, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX: ^IXIC) is down by more than 4% in that time.
Much of the sell-off is stemming from the tech sector, with artificial intelligence (AI) spending under the microscope. Rising bond yields have driven up borrowing costs, making it more expensive for AI hyperscalers to continue building data centers and related infrastructure. If big tech companies pull back on AI spending, it could cause a ripple effect across the broader market.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
At this point, it's too soon to tell whether this volatility is a blip on the radar or the beginning of a deeper drawdown. Regardless of what's coming, though, Warren Buffett has one tried-and-tested strategy that can set your portfolio up for success.
Image source: Getty Images. An industry's potential has limits
In a 1999 essay for Fortune , Warren Buffett issued a warning to investors. The stock market was reaping the rewards of the dot-com boom, with the S&P 500 surging by nearly 200% over the previous four years, but Buffett predicted stock prices would fall.
He also emphasized that when an industry is poised to transform society, it's especially important to choose your investments carefully. Buffett mentioned airlines as an example, noting that while air travel itself has had a monumental impact on our lives, 129 airlines had filed for bankruptcy over the previous 20 years.
Buffett's 1999 warning eventually rang true, as the dot-com bubble officially popped in early 2000 -- leading to a bear market that would last more than two years. Hundreds of tech stocks crashed and burned, despite the internet's revolutionary impact on the world.
"The key to investing is not assessing how much an industry is going to affect society, or how much it will grow," Buffett said in the Fortune essay, "but rather determining the competitive advantage of any given company and, above all, the durability of that advantage."
When the dot-com bubble burst, overvalued stocks crashed the hardest. These companies earned explosive returns when the bubble was building, but many had unsustainable business models, poorly managed finances, or inexperienced leadership teams that couldn't navigate the bear market.
Now, we could be facing a similar situation. AI, as a technology, could transform the world. But not every company in the AI space will thrive. Many tech stocks have seen eye-popping returns this year, but it's likely that at least a few of them have been driven by hype and are overvalued right now.
This doesn't mean that all stocks will struggle over time, though. Since the start of the dot-com bear market in March 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has soared by more than 715%. While many companies failed, some tech stocks of the era -- like Apple , Amazon , and Microsoft -- went on to become industry-leading giants.
Overvalued stocks from weak companies will be hit the hardest whenever the next bear market arrives. Companies with strong fundamentals and a durable competitive advantage, however, have the best chance at recovering and going on to earn positive long-term returns.
The single best move investors can make right now is to load up on quality stocks. The healthier your portfolio, the more likely it is to survive even a severe downturn. In Buffett's words: "The products or services that have wide, sustainable moats around them are the ones that deliver rewards to investors."

Kinder Morgan’s Natural Gas Pipeline Backlog Hits Record $13.2 Billion
Kinder Morgan reported record third-quarter 2026 earnings on Wednesday and announced $5.4 billion in new expansion projects, bringing its total project backlog to $14.4 billion, including a record $13.2 billion in natural gas infrastructure investments.
The Houston-based pipeline operator said its overall project backlog increased by a net $4.7 billion from the second quarter, after accounting for approximately $700 million in projects entering service.
The expansion reflects rising demand for natural gas infrastructure across the United States, particularly from power generation, data centers, industrial development, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
More than 75% of Kinder Morgan's total project backlog is tied to electricity generation and local gas distribution demand.
Two major natural gas pipeline projects account for a significant portion of the company's latest investment commitments.
The Southeast Connector Project, developed by Southern Natural Gas Company, will transport up to 2.6 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) of natural gas through approximately 470 miles of new pipeline and associated compression infrastructure.
The project will connect Marcellus and Utica shale gas supplies with expanding markets in the southeastern United States. Kinder Morgan expects its share of the investment to reach approximately $3.1 billion, with initial operations scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2030, subject to regulatory approvals.
Meanwhile, Natural Gas Pipeline Company of America has approved the Permian Link Project, a roughly $4.2 billion development designed to transport approximately 2.8 Bcf/d of natural gas.
The 434-mile pipeline will support new electricity generation serving a major hyperscale technology customer. Kinder Morgan's share of the investment is estimated at $1.6 billion, with startup targeted for the third quarter of 2030.
Both projects have secured long-term transportation agreements, providing contracted revenue streams once operational.
Kinder Morgan is also expanding its Creekside Lateral Project in Central Texas, approving an additional $150 million in development phases following new agreements with data center and industrial customers.
The approximately $235 million project is expected to supply more than 750 million cubic feet per day of contracted transportation capacity upon completion.
The company's expanding pipeline investment program comes alongside stronger operating performance.
Third-quarter net income climbed 22% to $764 million, compared with $628 million a year earlier. Adjusted earnings per share increased 21% to $0.35, while adjusted EBITDA rose 9% to $2.18 billion.
Natural gas transportation volumes increased 3% year over year, supported by higher LNG deliveries and increased demand across the company's Texas pipeline network. Natural gas gathering volumes climbed 14%, primarily reflecting stronger activity on the KinderHawk system.
The company now expects full-year adjusted EBITDA to exceed its original $8.6 billion budget by more than 6%, while adjusted earnings per share are projected to beat the initial $1.36 forecast by more than 13%.
Kinder Morgan also maintained its commitment to shareholder returns, declaring a quarterly dividend of $0.2975 per share, representing a 2% increase from the corresponding period last year.
Beyond natural gas, the company is advancing its Western Gateway refined products pipeline alongside Phillips 66 and HF Sinclair. The approximately 1,300-mile project is designed to deliver 230,000 barrels per day of transportation capacity to markets in Arizona and California, with operations targeted for 2029.
For investors, Kinder Morgan's growing inventory of contracted pipeline projects highlights the expanding role of natural gas infrastructure in meeting U.S. electricity demand, particularly as hyperscale data centers and industrial facilities drive new requirements for reliable power supplies.

DTEK then said Russia’s Feb. 3 assault “dealt the most powerful blow to the energy sector since the beginning of the year,” WP reported .
From early October 2025 through mid‑January 2026, Ukraine’s intelligence service logged 256 drone and missile strikes on Ukrainian energy facilities: 11 on hydroelectric plants, 94 on thermal plants and 151 on substations. Ukraine’s then energy minister Denys Shmyhal said on Jan. 16 that “there is not a single power plant in Ukraine that the enemy has not attacked” and that “thousands of megawatts of generation have been knocked out,” according to The New Yorker .
Every power plant in Ukraine has been damaged by Russian attacks, according to Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s February 2026 estimate .

Ukrainian energy expert Oleksandr Kharchenko estimated in March 2026 that restoring Ukraine’s full electrical and heating capacity would require years. “In the best-case scenario, we will be able to restore maybe 30 or 40% of electrical capacity before next winter,” he estimated according to a NYT March 30, 2026 report.
Energy blackouts, which have been caused by Russian attacks, have cut economic growth in Ukraine by 2.5 percentage points so far in 2026, according to a May 2026 estimate by the Economist .

In the three weeks preceding Aug. 18, 2026, Russian strikes on Ukrainian warehouses had cost Ukrainian businesses $500 million, according to an Aug. 18, 2026, estimate by The Economist .
Russian strikes have destroyed about 90% of Ukraine’s food-logistics infrastructure, according to an Aug. 30, 2026 estimate by Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi.
Russia’s air campaign has destroyed about 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s 5 million square meters of modern warehouse space, including 900,000 square meters in recent months, according to a Sept. 20, 2026, estimate by Financial Times .
Ukraine’s economy ministry estimates the damage from Russian attacks will reach approximately $10 billion by the end of 2026, while EBRD cut its growth forecast for Ukraine from 2.2% to 1.5% with some economists expecting zero growth, according to a Sept. 25, 2026, report by NYT . The Russian strikes also disabled Ukraine’s three remaining major steel plants responsible for 90% of national output, according to the Sept. 20, 2026, estimate by Financial Times .

items.title: Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
items.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
items.content:
Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Zelenskyy says early warning system for Russian missile attacks resumes
Rescuers with a search dog look for victims among the rubble of a house after a Russian air attack in Kharkiv, Ukraine, Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.
KYIV, Ukraine — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that Kyiv is once again receiving early warnings from its partners about incoming Russian missiles following recent strikes that he said occurred without enough notice, leaving civilians vulnerable.
A conversation with President Volodmyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine
For at least a week, the Ukrainian leader has said that his country has not received early warnings about ballistic missiles aimed at the capital. Such intelligence, he said, saves lives by allowing the public to be alerted and giving military units time to try to intercept the missiles.
Zelenskyy said the change happened after talks with his American counterparts, including a phone call with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
"We are thankful that intelligence works now, and I'm speaking about early warning, which is very important for our people, for children, adults, civilians, because we can hear when ballistic is coming," Zelenskyy said on a visit to Norway. "So we are thankful to American side now that it works."
Speaking to reporters in India, Rubio acknowledged mutual frustration between the U.S. and Ukraine over intelligence sharing and weapons supplies but emphatically denied that the Trump administration has made any changes to previous policy on either issue.
In other developments, Russia unleashed another missile and drone blitz of civilian areas in Ukraine, killing at least nine people, officials said, as Zelenskyy sought more American and European help.
Zelenskyy was joined in Norway by U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, who has tried without success to steer Russia and Ukraine toward a settlement to end the war. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb also met with the Ukrainian president in Norway's capital.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyj, Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, and Finnish President Alexander Stubb speak during a press conference on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026 in Oslo, Norway.
Gahr Støre said Witkoff planned to fly to St. Petersburg on Wednesday to meet with Russian leaders, exchange ideas from the Oslo meeting and share proposals from European and American colleagues.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Moscow is willing to listen to new U.S. proposals about Ukraine but doesn't expect any "miracle" from Washington.
Trump makes Russia-friendly moves as he looks for a way to end the war with Ukraine
At the White House, President Donald Trump stepped up the pressure on Zelenskyy to come to an agreement with Russia as relations between the two men have soured again.
"We want Zelenskyy to make a deal," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. "We've given a lot to Ukraine. We've gotten absolutely nothing back except grief, death, tremendous monetary loss."
If that doesn't happen, "I think it's going to be a very bad thing."
The conversation with Rubio came after Zelenskyy told a bipartisan group of U.S. lawmakers Monday that he believes "some political decision has been made to slow down ... support for us."
Ukraine has nearly run out of American-made Patriot air-defense interceptors that it needs to stop Russian ballistic missiles, according to Zelenskyy, who has pleaded for Washington to send more. But he said the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles that other countries have purchased for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian leader also said speed restrictions were still in place on his country's use of Starshield, the military-grade version of U.S. company SpaceX's satellite internet service Starlink, hampering battlefield operations.
Trump also has waived sanctions on Russia, a move that Zelenskyy slammed as helping Putin push on with Moscow's full-scale invasion, which will hit the five-year mark in February.
Ukraine and the U.S. are at odds over Starshield. Here's what to know
Zelenskyy said he had "a substantive conversation" with Rubio.
"I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," Zelenskyy said on social media.
Rubio, who arrived Tuesday in India on an official trip, denied that the U.S. is withholding assistance from Ukraine.
The Patriot ammunition Ukraine needs is in short supply and is also required elsewhere in the world, Rubio said.
"There has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," he said.
European countries, worried about Russia's plans on the continent and viewing Ukraine as a bulwark against Moscow's ambitions, are trying to take up the slack of any falloff in U.S. supplies, but some key assets are American-made.
European countries and European Union institutions have allocated 237 billion euros ($266 billion) to support Ukraine, compared with 115 billion euros ($129 billion) from the U.S., according to Germany's Kiel Institute, which tracks assistance to Kyiv.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on Tuesday questioned whether U.S. negotiators have been honest brokers in peace efforts. Ukrainian officials say the Trump administration has encouraged Kyiv to surrender land to Russia in return for peace.
"Although American negotiators have been trying to push Ukraine into surrender for … one and a half years now," Ukraine has not surrendered on Putin's terms "because Europe has been supporting Ukraine," Kallas said.
Russian attacks cause power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions
Four people were killed and 27 others wounded, including children, in Russian missile and drone attacks on the Kyiv region over the past day, regional police said.
Three were killed and six were wounded in the Obukhiv district, where warehouses were damaged, police said. In the Bucha district, one woman was killed and 21 people were wounded, eight of them children, while hundreds of buildings were damaged, according to police.
On Tuesday morning, three people were killed and four injured when two vehicles caught fire in a Russian attack on the Kyiv-Odesa highway, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. The dead included the driver of a shuttle bus that was hit. The bus transports people from Kyiv to the National Military Memorial Cemetery.
Two more people were killed in a Russian attack Tuesday on warehouses on the outskirts of Dnipro in central Ukraine, authorities said.
National grid operator Ukrenergo reported power outages in 12 regions of Ukraine following the Russian attacks.
The Russian Defense Ministry said in a statement that its forces carried out drone strikes on logistics centers, port infrastructure and three cargo ships in the port of Reni in the Odesa region. It said that another bulk carrier was hit at sea on its way to Odesa.
Meanwhile, air defenses intercepted 136 Ukrainian drones over multiple Russian regions overnight, the ministry said.

items.title: Qatar, France call for opening of Hormuz and Gaza ceasefire implementation
items.summary: Qatari and French leaders stress need to restore freedom of navigation in Strait of Hormuz.
items.content:
Share Qatar, France call for opening of Hormuz and Gaza ceasefire implementation on social media
Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani looks on alongside Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani and French President Emmanuel Macron at the Rosewood Hotel in Lusail, Qatar, on October 21, 2026 [Benoit Tessier/Reuters]
Qatar and France have called for freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the implementation of the so-called ceasefire in Gaza, after the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, met French President Emmanuel Macron in Doha.
A joint statement on Wednesday said the two leaders stressed the importance of restoring freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz “without constraints or fees”.
list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Macron lines up more Gulf diesel as France battles soaring fuel prices
list 2 of 3 As Macron visits Gulf, can France forge its own energy-for-security future?
list 3 of 3 Iran’s enriched uranium re-emerges as point of contention in US talks
Qatari mediator Ibrahim bin Sultan Al Hashmi had said on Tuesday that diplomatic efforts are ongoing to de-escalate regional tensions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Wednesday that “Iran is prepared to give diplomacy another chance.”
“The two leaders condemned Iranian military attacks against countries in the region which constitute a serious breach of international law,” according to the Qatari-French statement.
The two leaders also called for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza “in accordance with the agreed arrangements”, as well as the urgent, safe and unhindered delivery of humanitarian aid “without conditions or restrictions”.
The United Nations World Food Programme (WFP) said on Monday that about 1.4 million people in Gaza, roughly two-thirds of the population, face acute food insecurity at crisis levels or worse.
“France and Qatar reiterated their opposition to any annexation of the West Bank and called for an end to Israeli settlement policies and settler violence,” the statement added.
On Lebanon, the two countries backed full implementation of the Trilateral Framework Agreement to restore Lebanese sovereignty, disarm Hezbollah and secure a complete Israeli withdrawal.
They also warned against a security vacuum following the end of the UN peacekeeping mission’s mandate, calling for continued international support for Lebanese authorities and armed forces.
On Syria, both countries said they were ready to jointly support stabilisation and economic recovery projects in coordination with Syrian authorities.
Beyond regional issues, Qatar and France agreed to expand defence, security and economic cooperation.
Macron’s regional tour, which also included Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, aimed to strengthen strategic and economic partnerships and support efforts to restore regional stability and freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

items.content:
Witkoff calls Putin a ‘humanitarian’ after release of jailed American – video
Putin orders release of jailed American as he meets Trump envoy for Ukraine talks
Russia frees Stephen Hubbard after US request while Steve Witkoff praises Putin, wanted by ICC as war criminal, as a ‘humanitarian’
Vladimir Putin ordered the release of an American man from a Russian jail as he met Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in St Petersburg on Wednesday for fresh talks on ending the war in Ukraine, amid increasingly close relations between Moscow and Washington.
Trump had previously asked Putin to free Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old former teacher who had spent more than four years in Russian jails on charges of fighting as a mercenary for Ukraine .
His release appeared to be Moscow’s latest calculated move to bring Trump further into line with Putin’s position on Ukraine , while offering the US president a diplomatic victory before the midterm elections.
Hubbard was released unilaterally by Russia , rather than as part of a prisoner exchange as has often been the case with previous releases of Americans held in the country.
Writing on social media after the release was announced, Trump said it followed a request he had made “directly” to Putin last week.
He wrote on Truth Social: “The United States, out of respect for President Trump, was not required to give anything in return – an unprecedented situation for Russia … There was no ‘swap’ necessary for this release.”
Stephen Hubbard in court in Moscow in October 2024. Photograph: Moscow city court press service/AP\ Hubbard’s younger sister told the Associated Press she had spoken to her brother, who said he had thought he was “going to die in prison”.
“He’s out of Russia territory. He is free, praise God,” Patricia Hubbard Fox said, adding that her brother suffered beatings and starvation while he was held captive.
Witkoff, meanwhile, lavished praise on Putin during their meeting at the grand Constantine Palace in St Petersburg, describing the Russian president as a humanitarian.
“You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff told Putin. He also conveyed Trump’s thanks for a deal to resume Russian diesel exports to the US.
The Russian president is wanted by the international criminal court (ICC) as a war criminal, in relation to the deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia during the war.
More than 17,500 civilians have been confirmed killed in Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to the UN, which says the true toll is likely to be significantly higher.
The warmth of Witkoff’s remarks stood in stark contrast to the increasingly hostile rhetoric directed at Volodymyr Zelenskyy by senior US officials, most notably Trump, who has called for the Ukrainian president to resign and portrayed him as the main obstacle to peace.
Witkoff travelled to Russia from Oslo, where he had met Zelenskyy and European leaders a day earlier in an attempt to inject momentum into stalled negotiations, with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year.
Witkoff told Putin during a televised portion of their meeting: “We’ve brought some papers. It’s really some ideas, some sort of peace deal between Russia and Ukraine, and you’ll read that at your leisure.”
The visit was Witkoff’s ninth to Russia since Trump tasked him with brokering an end to the war.
Witkoff described his meeting with Putin as “constructive” but said “important work” remained and trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine “at the technical level” would follow.
The Kremlin said it had agreed “in principle” to the talks, which would focus on how to guarantee the security of Ukraine and Russia once the war ended.
‘You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,’ Witkoff told Putin during their meeting. Photograph: Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP The latest rupture in relations between Washington and Kyiv was triggered by Trump’s surprise decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal with Putin, followed by his call for Zelenskyy to be replaced after Ukraine refused to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Kyiv has since complained of disruptions to US intelligence-sharing and restrictions on its access to Starshield , the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite network.
Zelenskyy said on Tuesday that Washington had resumed providing advance warnings of Russian missile attacks after his meeting with Witkoff in Oslo.
But Ukraine continues to face restrictions on Starshield, although it remains unclear who ordered them. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk had personally ordered the slowdown, while Reuters, citing sources, said the directive had come from inside the White House.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Wednesday that the decision to restrict Ukraine’s access came from Musk.
“I’m not aware that we knew ​about this decision beforehand. But that’s irrelevant,” Rubio told reporters ‌during a trip to India.
“The bottom ‌line is that, that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds ‌they’ll allow it to be used at.”
‘Drones all night. By morning, you smell the smoke’: life in the last hotel on Ukraine’s frontline
During Wednesday’s meeting with Witkoff, Putin thanked Trump and his wife, Melania, for “their attention to efforts to end the war”.
Yet there are few signs of an imminent breakthrough. Despite repeated Ukrainian calls for a ceasefire, including a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure, Moscow has given little indication that it intends to end its bombardment of Ukraine as winter approaches, apparently confident that continued pressure will help it extract greater concessions from Kyiv.
The Russian leader remains intent on sticking to his maximalist war aims, including his demand for full Russian control of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region.
Putin also sought to emphasise the prospects for closer economic ties between Russia and the US once the war ends, suggesting that Moscow could significantly increase its exports of fertilisers to the American market.
Russian officials said the first tanker carrying diesel to the US would depart on Thursday as part of an initial shipment of about 300,000 tonnes.
Energy analysts and traders have questioned whether Trump’s agreement to temporarily resume Russian diesel imports will deliver meaningful relief to US consumers before the midterm elections, arguing that the volumes involved are too small to significantly ease the global supply squeeze.
The talks on Wednesday also touched on a possible meeting in China next month between Putin, Trump and the Chinese president, Xi Jinping. The Kremlin said Beijing was already making preparations for what it described as an unprecedented summit between the three leaders.

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot  gold prices were higher in late U.S. trading Wednesday, while spot  silver recovered from earlier losses, as a softer U.S. dollar and easing crude oil prices provided some support for precious metals despite persistent inflation concerns and expectations for additional Federal Reserve tightening. Strong corporate earnings lifted major U.S. stock indexes, while unresolved tensions involving Iran and the Strait of Hormuz continued to complicate the outlook for energy prices and monetary policy. Gold was trading near $4,141.01 an ounce, up 0.66%, while silver was near $57.976, up 0.34%, in the latest available late-session market readings.
The latest U.S. economic reports continue to point to weakness in interest rate-sensitive sectors of the economy. September housing starts declined 5.2% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 1.221 million units , below expectations of approximately 1.305 million and down from an upwardly revised 1.288 million in August. Building permits slipped 0.2% to 1.400 million units, while single-family starts declined 4.6% to 859,000 units. Pending home sales fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% from a year earlier, reinforcing concerns that high mortgage rates and weakening household confidence are restraining residential investment. Wednesday's weekly U.S. petroleum inventory report also highlighted the continuing tightness in energy markets, with commercial crude oil stocks declining 3.1 million barrels to 412.5 million barrels, compared with expectations for a draw of approximately 300,000 barrels. Gasoline inventories fell 3.0 million barrels, while distillate stocks increased 1.7 million barrels.
The Federal Reserve remains in its premeeting communications blackout, leaving incoming economic releases as the principal influence on near-term interest rate expectations. Thursday brings weekly initial jobless claims at 8:30 a.m. EDT, followed Friday by preliminary October manufacturing and services purchasing managers' indexes at 9:45 a.m. EDT and the final University of Michigan consumer sentiment survey at 10 a.m. EDT. Traders will be particularly sensitive to signs of weakening labor-market conditions and changes in consumer inflation expectations ahead of next week's Fed decision. Softer employment and business activity data could reduce December tightening expectations and support gold through lower Treasury yields and a weaker dollar, while stronger readings or renewed inflation pressure would reinforce the argument for maintaining restrictive monetary policy.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a significant source of uncertainty Wednesday, although crude oil prices eased as traders balanced continued military and shipping risks against signs of a recovery in regional petroleum exports. Attacks on vessels in the Persian Gulf and threats against Saudi Arabian infrastructure have maintained concerns about the reliability of energy shipments, while diplomatic contacts involving Washington and Tehran have yet to produce a confirmed agreement. Total crude exports from the Persian Gulf and alternative shipping routes have recovered to approximately 24 million barrels per day, exceeding prewar volumes, although roughly 40% of regional shipments now bypass the Strait of Hormuz, compared with 17% before the conflict. Direct traffic through the waterway remains disrupted, and continuing security threats, higher shipping costs and uncertainty about U.S.-Iran negotiations have prevented crude prices from returning to pre-conflict levels. December WTI futures settled at $97.15 a barrel, down 0.7%, while Brent crude finished near $108.82.
For gold, the decline in crude oil prices has eased some immediate inflation and interest rate pressure, while continuing uncertainty about Gulf security provides an underlying source of defensive demand. However, the recovery in broader equity markets and expectations for additional Fed tightening have limited the metal's safe-haven appeal. Silver has remained more sensitive to concerns about industrial demand and the direction of real interest rates, with recent price action reflecting profit-taking after Tuesday's advance. The contrasting pressures of geopolitical risk, weaker economic activity and still-elevated inflation expectations continue to complicate the outlook for both precious metals.
North American equity markets finished higher Wednesday, supported by strong corporate earnings and renewed buying interest in technology and artificial intelligence-related shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 360.21 points, or 0.69%, to close at 52,856.09, while the S&P 500 advanced 44.60 points, or 0.58%, to 7,757.17. The Nasdaq Composite climbed 278.04 points, or 1.05%, to 26,702.86, leading the major benchmarks higher as technology stocks recovered from last week's selling pressure. The Russell 2000 advanced 7.60 points, or 0.27%, to 2,781.02. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also strengthened, rising 0.76% to close at 36,382.77, with broader equity sentiment benefiting from the recovery in U.S. shares. Better-than-expected corporate results helped offset concerns about elevated financing costs, artificial intelligence investment valuations and persistent geopolitical uncertainty.
European equity markets were mixed Wednesday as investors assessed corporate earnings, elevated energy prices and mounting fiscal concerns in France. The pan-European Stoxx 600 traded near unchanged during the session, while Germany's DAX slipped approximately 0.1% and France's CAC 40 gained around 0.1% in the latest independently confirmed market readings. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 declined approximately 0.2%, pressured by weaker mining shares. Corporate results produced sharp individual stock movements, with strong earnings supporting European technology and consumer companies while disappointing guidance weighed on retailers. The selloff in French government bonds remained another source of concern, with the country's benchmark 10-year yield rising above 5.0% for the first time since 2002. The spread over equivalent German government debt widened to approximately 157 basis points, reflecting growing investor unease about France's fiscal position and political instability.
The key outside markets see Nymex December WTI crude oil futures lower and settling at $97.15 a barrel, while Brent crude finished near $108.82. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note remained near the 5.1% area. items.summary: Critical PHP security flaws trigger global warnings as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond to potential cyber threats.
items.content:
Critical web security flaws spark global alarm: Google, OpenAI, Amazon
Two critical vulnerabilities, collectively known as “PHP2Shell,” could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers.
Governments worldwide have issued urgent security warnings, while Google, OpenAI and other tech companies have worked to identify vulnerabilities and protect affected systems.
Amazon detected attempts to exploit the flaws before their public disclosure, but said it remains unclear how attackers obtained information about them.
21 October 2026, Baden-Württemberg, Stuttgart: When visiting the website of the Baden-Württemberg Ministry of the Interior, a warning message appears in the browser indicating a potential security issue. A serious security vulnerability is threatening websites worldwide; blogs, online stores, and news portals could become targets for attackers. The PHP vulnerability allows attackers to take over entire servers. Photo: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa (Photo by Bernd Weißbrod/picture alliance via Getty Images)
The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.
The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.
The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.
The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.
Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore , the United Kingdom , Australia , Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems.
Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.
Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.
OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.
The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.
Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.
The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

US Stock Futures Edge Higher as SpaceX and Tesla Explore Merger and Meta Earnings Approach: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq, Wall Street
Wall Street NYSE stock exchange ©Shutterstock US stock futures traded mostly higher on Wednesday as investors assessed corporate earnings, developments in artificial intelligence investment and geopolitical uncertainty surrounding the conflict in the Middle East. Attention also turned to comments from Elon Musk about a potential merger between SpaceX and Tesla, reports concerning Anthropic's financial performance and Meta Platforms' forthcoming quarterly results.
US futures rise as investors assess earnings and oil prices
At 03:01 ET (07:01 GMT), S&P 500 futures were up 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures gained 148 points, or 0.5%. Dow Jones futures were broadly unchanged.
Wall Street ended Tuesday's session with mixed results. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average advanced, while the Nasdaq Composite closed slightly lower.
Oil prices fluctuated during the session following unconfirmed reports that Qatar and Pakistan had proposed renewed negotiations aimed at ending the conflict involving Iran. Brent crude briefly declined from approximately $112 to $106 per barrel before recovering.
The initial decline in energy prices coincided with gains in equities, which have recently been affected by concerns over borrowing costs and the scale of debt-financed investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
"The relief from energy that played out late in the European session meant equities rallied as investors overcame some of their earlier AI jitters," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a research note.
Brent subsequently returned to approximately $110 per barrel after reports of comments attributed to Iran's president concerning the possibility of further US military action.
Technology shares underperformed parts of the broader market. An index tracking semiconductor companies declined 0.29%, although it recovered much of its earlier losses. AI cloud infrastructure provider CoreWeave (NASDAQ:CRWV) also rebounded during the session.
SpaceX and Tesla establish committees to examine possible merger
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) have formed committees to evaluate a potential combination of the two businesses, according to Elon Musk, who serves as chief executive of both companies.
Speaking to investors following SpaceX's quarterly earnings announcement, Musk said the committees had not reached an agreement on "the terms of any transaction."
Musk, who is not a member of either committee, said there was "no guarantee" that a merger would take place, although he considered there to be "a lot of merit" in combining the businesses.
Shares in both companies advanced in after-hours trading following the comments.
A potential transaction would bring together SpaceX's rocket launch and satellite operations with Tesla's electric vehicle and related technology businesses. No transaction terms or timetable have been announced.
SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.6 billion, an increase of more than 160% compared with the previous year and above analysts' expectations.
The company recorded profit of $4.4 billion, while capital expenditure reached $19.6 billion during the period.
The results marked SpaceX's second quarterly earnings publication since its initial public offering earlier in 2026.
Tesla is scheduled to report its quarterly financial results after Wednesday's market close.
Anthropic reports revenue growth alongside financial and operational risks
Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANTP) reported substantial revenue growth during the first half of the year, according to media reports citing disclosures associated with its potential initial public offering.
The company, which develops the Claude AI models, generated revenue of $16.3 billion during the six-month period.
Approximately 20% of that revenue came from two customers, highlighting the concentration of sales among a relatively small number of clients.
Anthropic indicated that a significant proportion of its revenue is expected to remain dependent on a limited customer base for the foreseeable future.
The company also identified uncertainty surrounding access to the computing infrastructure required to develop and operate its AI models.
Anthropic recorded a net loss exceeding $80 billion, compared with a loss of $13 billion in the corresponding period last year. The reported increase was largely attributed to an accounting adjustment.
Additional risks identified in the disclosures included potential legal liabilities arising from the use of artificial intelligence, including cybersecurity-related incidents.
Reports suggested that a future stock market listing could value Anthropic at approximately $2 trillion, although no confirmed IPO valuation was provided.
Meta earnings to provide update on AI investment plans
Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) is scheduled to release its quarterly earnings after Wednesday's closing bell, with investors focusing on revenue performance and the company's spending plans for artificial intelligence.
The owner of Facebook and Instagram has recently expanded its AI product portfolio following the September introduction of its Muse model.
According to the reported information, the product attracted millions of downloads following its launch, with applications including travel booking assistance and tools for small businesses.
Meta subsequently introduced an open-weight version of its Muse Spark model for coding applications.
The earnings announcement will provide an update on Meta's investment requirements as it expands its AI infrastructure and related services.
Large technology companies have committed substantial capital to advanced semiconductor purchases, computing capacity and data centre construction as they develop AI products.
Investors have increasingly focused on the relationship between these expenditures, financing requirements and the revenue generated by AI-related services.
Meta's results will therefore be examined for information on capital expenditure expectations and the financial contribution of its AI initiatives.
Nvidia reportedly considers additional investment in Firmus Grid
Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) is in discussions about investing hundreds of millions of dollars in Australian AI cloud infrastructure company Firmus Grid, according to a report by The Information.
Nvidia already holds an investment stake in Firmus and has invested in several other companies operating in the AI cloud infrastructure sector.
The reported discussions follow Firmus Grid's decision to abandon plans for an initial public offering in Australia earlier this month.
The company cited recent financial market volatility as a reason for withdrawing the proposed listing, which it said would not have been in shareholders' interests under the prevailing conditions.
Firmus had previously outlined plans for an IPO at a valuation exceeding $30 billion, potentially making it one of Australia's largest stock market listings.
The size, structure and timing of any additional Nvidia investment have not been confirmed.
US equity markets entered Wednesday's session with attention divided between corporate earnings, AI infrastructure financing and developments in the Middle East. The forthcoming results from Meta and Tesla, together with reported activity involving SpaceX, Anthropic and Nvidia, are among the company-specific developments being assessed by investors.

items.content:
Wall Street Futures Rise as Corporate Earnings Support Technology Stocks: Dow Jones, S&P, Nasdaq
Nasdaq sign on a tall building ©Dries Buytaert US stock index futures pointed to a higher opening on Wednesday, suggesting Wall Street could extend its gains from recent sessions as investors assessed quarterly earnings reports and prepared for further results from major technology companies.
Technology stocks were expected to contribute to the early advance, although individual companies recorded contrasting pre-market movements following their latest financial announcements.
SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX) shares rose 8.8% in pre-market trading after the rocket and space technology company led by Elon Musk reported third-quarter earnings above market expectations, supported by a substantial increase in revenue.
Musk also confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA) had established independent special committees to examine a potential merger. No final decision regarding a transaction was announced.
Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) advanced 12.2% before the opening bell after the data centre server manufacturer raised its revenue outlook for the first quarter of its fiscal year.
In contrast, Netflix (NASDAQ:NFLX) declined 6.8% in pre-market trading. The streaming company reported third-quarter earnings that exceeded analysts' estimates but issued revenue guidance below market expectations.
AT&T (NYSE:T) shares also fell, losing 5% despite the telecommunications company reporting third-quarter revenue and earnings above forecasts.
Investors were also awaiting quarterly results from Tesla, Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) and IBM (NYSE:IBM), all scheduled for release after Wednesday's market close.
The anticipated higher opening followed a mixed performance on Wall Street on Tuesday, when stocks recovered from an initial decline before giving back part of their gains later in the session.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 529.85 points, or 1%, to close at 52,495.88, its highest closing level in more than a month. The S&P 500 gained 21.84 points, or 0.3%, to 7,712.57, while the Nasdaq Composite slipped 6.07 points, or less than 0.1%, to 26,424.82.
Industrial conglomerate 3M (NYSE:MMM) contributed to the Dow's advance, with its shares rising 6% after the company reported third-quarter earnings above expectations and increased its full-year profit forecast.
Other Dow constituents, including Amgen (NASDAQ:AMGN), Merck (NYSE:MRK) and UnitedHealth (NYSE:UNH), also recorded gains.
Movements in energy prices influenced trading sentiment during Tuesday's session. US crude oil futures fell substantially after earlier increases, following a report suggesting that diplomatic efforts could lead to a reduction in tensions between the United States and Iran.
According to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, negotiators from Qatar and Pakistan had presented a compromise proposal aimed at ending the conflict. The report cited a source suggesting that an announcement concerning a possible halt to the escalation could come during the week.
Neither the United States nor Iran had confirmed the reported proposal.
The decline in crude oil prices coincided with increased buying interest in equities, although investors remained attentive to geopolitical developments and forthcoming corporate earnings.
Among individual sectors, pharmaceutical stocks advanced, lifting the NYSE Arca Pharmaceutical Index by 2.8% to its highest closing level in two months.
Housing-related shares also gained, with the Philadelphia Housing Sector Index rising 2.6%.
Biotechnology, healthcare and airline stocks recorded increases alongside most other major market sectors.
Wednesday's session is expected to remain focused on corporate earnings, particularly the forthcoming announcements from Tesla, Meta Platforms and IBM, while developments in energy markets and US-Iran relations could also influence investor sentiment.

A 2027 turning point? Goldman, Citi see stabilising signs in China’s housing market
Encouraging holiday sales and shrinking supply point to recovery for country’s property sector, according to Goldman Sachs and Citi
As China’s housing market downturn enters its fifth year, global investment banks including Goldman Sachs and Citi say they expect the sector to pivot as soon as 2027, with expectations fuelled by signs of shrinking supply and robust sales over the National Day holiday in early October.
Citi holds a positive view on the sector and saw 2027 as a pivotal year for home price recovery in Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. Home prices in China hit their lowest point in June 2024, according to Citi.
Shanghai became the first city to post positive year-on-year growth in secondary home prices in September, with prices rising 0.8 per cent, according to the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday.
“While we need further confirmation before declaring a sustained recovery, the evidence increasingly points to stabilising and potentially rising home prices in top cities, with most tier-two cities likely to lag,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research, in a report on Tuesday.
